strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence of limitations in existing systems (Figures 2-4, Tables 1-2)
Strong theoretical insight via Proposition 1 showing API return length can dominate total length in determining request completion time

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (GPT-J-6B, OPT-13B), GPUs (RTX 4090, H800, A100), datasets (Merge, ToolBench), and workload types (Poisson, fixed, Gamma) with extensive metrics (goodput, TTFT, normalized latency, SLO attainment, P95 metrics, TPOT)
Thoughtful two-stage system design combining prediction-driven scheduling (Stage I) with runtime correction (Stage II) to mitigate prediction errors
Substantial practical improvements: 4.7-33.1× effective throughput over vLLM, 3.3-13.2× over InferCept, up to 96.3% TTFT reduction across all configurations
Ablation studies and robustness analysis demonstrating complementary benefits of scheduling and dynamic batching components
Clear presentation with informative figures and comprehensive algorithm specification in appendix
weaknesses: Prediction model performance inadequately validated: 65% accuracy on Merge and 85% on ToolBench without sensitivity analysis showing impact on system performance with degraded prediction quality

No theoretical justification for cost formulation in Equations 9-12 and 16-19; design choices (e.g., quadratic terms in prefill cost) appear heuristic without principled derivation or empirical validation

Numerous design parameters (α for anti-starvation, β_low/β_high for batching bounds, γ for preemptible memory, M for KV memory footprint) lack systematic sensitivity analysis or clear specification of values used in experiments, hindering reproducibility

Dynamic batching validation incomplete: ablation in Figure 10 shown only for 2 load levels; bounded constraint mechanism appears ad-hoc without ablation showing contribution or guidance on setting β values

Limited scope and potential unfair comparisons: system designed specifically for augmented LLMs with APIs; vLLM baseline appears unoptimized; no comparison with other scheduling approaches (SJF, LJF, ML-based schedulers) from broader literature despite citing them

Stage I approximation for Preserve policy uses pre-invocation cost to estimate behavior during API call, which could be highly inaccurate for long or unpredictable API durations without impact quantification

Missing robustness analysis: GPU memory safety mechanisms when dynamic batching produces token_budget exceeding available memory not discussed; formal fairness guarantees or starvation prevention proofs absent

Experimental rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing; number of independent runs and variance between runs not reported; SLO value choices (TTFT < 1s) not justified or sensitivity-tested

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and demonstrates limitations of FCFS/SJF scheduling for augmented LLM inference through concrete examples and empirical evidence (Figures 2-4, Table 1)

Sound technical approach: Request lifecycle modeling elegantly captures multi-stage execution; space-time cost model provides principled resource accounting; state-aware feedback refinement mitigates prediction errors

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Diverse testbed (4 models, 3 GPU types, 2 datasets), multiple baselines (vLLM, INFERCEPT, SSJF, MARS), rich metrics (goodput, TTFT, latency, P95/P99, SLO attainment), thorough ablations and robustness tests
Strong empirical results: 6.5× goodput over vLLM, 4.7× over INFERCEPT, 95.6% TTFT reduction; latency breakdown shows gains from queuing time reduction; improvements consistent across diverse settings

Practical design with low overhead: Prediction module adds <0.1% cost; scheduling overhead remains at millisecond level even with hundreds of paused requests; implementation integrated with production system (vLLM)

Adaptive scheduling with runtime refinement: Pre-invocation estimation with post-invocation feedback cleverly handles prediction errors; dynamic batch budgeting considers reclaimable memory from paused requests
weaknesses: Limited theoretical analysis: Approximation guarantee (Theorem E.1) only applies to simplified per-iteration problem with fixed costs; full algorithm with evolving costs, stochastic call returns, and continuous feedback lacks formal guarantees

Prediction accuracy and generalization risks: Output length (65-85% bucket accuracy) and call duration (0.4-5s MSE) predictions are moderate; at 40-50% error injection, TTFT still increases 10-20s (Figure 8); no analysis by request type; BERT model may not transfer to new workloads

Limited experimental scope: Only two benchmark datasets (INFERCEPT, ToolBench); no real production traces or datacenter workloads; homogeneous external call patterns; fixed SLO values; unclear real-world applicability

Hyperparameter tuning without guidance: β parameter requires manual tuning (Table 5); clipping bounds and per-token memory footprint need per-hardware/model configuration; no adaptive mechanism provided

Cost model simplifications and unvalidated assumptions: Space-time cost assumes piecewise constant memory; context-handling policy selection uses heuristic waste formulas (Eq. 12-14) rather than empirical measurements; resumption cost assumptions may not hold across hardware/models; no empirical validation of cost model accuracy

Incremental novelty: Combines existing techniques (value-density greedy knapsack, INFERCEPT's Preserve/Swap/Discard policies, BERT-based prediction) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts; main contribution is their integration for augmented LLM inference

Missing generalization analysis: Approach is LLM-specific; applicability to other inference workloads, distributed serving, or multi-tenant scenarios unclear; no study of requests with data-dependent external call decisions

Presentation and design justification issues: Heavy notation (Table 4); limited intuition for space-time cost vs. alternatives; gap between optimization formulation (Eq. 3) and greedy algorithm; waste metric not validated for scheduling context specifically
